Subject: Service Center Staffing Review and Assignment Plan

Overview
We are conducting a staffing review to align our multi-skilled workforce with station-level customer demand across the service center. The operation comprises multiple service stations supported by several staff types with different skills, speeds, and costs. Our objective is to place the right people at the right stations, hour by hour, to ensure reliable service at the lowest feasible cost.

Current Situation
- Each service station experiences a steady stream of customers, with known arrival volumes by hour.
- Staff types differ in how quickly they can handle customers at each station, measured as average minutes per customer. These speeds vary by both station and skill.
- Not every staff type can work at every station; a subset of station–skill pairings are restricted due to qualifications or policy.
- Each staff type has a distinct hourly cost, and the available headcount for each type is limited.
- Every station requires a baseline presence for coverage at all times, independent of demand spikes.

Staffing Challenge
The assignment space is large: many stations can be staffed by multiple skill types, but some pairings are off-limits. Handling times range from quick, transactional interactions to longer, more complex engagements, while arrival volumes span from moderate to very busy across stations and hours. Without a disciplined allocation, we risk either long lines and missed commitments (if we under-assign) or unnecessary idle time and waste (if we over-assign).

Service Quality and Policy Requirements
- Utilization policy: Staff should not be busy all the time. We impose a target cap on how much of their time can be occupied. Practically, this means the combined capacity of people assigned to a station should comfortably outpace expected arrivals, providing a buffer for variability, exceptions, and breaks.
- Coverage minimums: Every station must be staffed with at least a minimum number of people for visibility, safety, and continuity.
- Qualifications: Some station–skill pairings are not permitted; these must be respected in any plan.
- Availability and cost: We must stay within the available headcount for each staff type and be mindful of their distinct hourly costs.

Key Considerations
- Aligning units: Demand arrives as customers per hour, while handling speed is tracked as minutes per customer. When we plan capacity, we evaluate how many customers a given staffing mix can reasonably handle each hour based on those handling times.
- Trade-offs: Faster, higher-cost staff may achieve throughput with fewer seats; slower, lower-cost staff may require more seats to meet the same demand. The best mix depends on demand, the utilization cap, and availability.
- Bottlenecks: Restricted pairings and limited headcount can create pinch points at certain stations; anticipating these is critical to avoid service gaps.
- Operational resilience: Minimum coverage and utilization caps also protect breaks, rotations, and surge handling without dropping below safe staffing.

Goal
Determine the station-by-station staffing mix—how many people of each staff type to assign to each station—that:
- Meets or exceeds expected arrivals with a reasonable buffer dictated by our utilization policy;
- Satisfies minimum coverage and respects qualification restrictions;
- Stays within available headcount; and
- Minimizes total hourly staffing cost across the service center.

Next Steps
- Validate station arrival profiles and skill-specific handling times with station leads.
- Confirm the qualification matrix (restricted station–skill pairings) and any temporary waivers.
- Verify available headcount and hourly cost for each staff type.
- Develop and review the recommended staffing allocation, with sensitivity checks for higher-than-expected arrivals.
- Align with Scheduling and HR on implementation, training, and rotation plans.
